newsitem.title: USA: Storm edges over Western U.S., flooding feared.
newsitem.headline: Storm edges over Western U.S., flooding feared.

text.p: A powerful storm inched out of the Pacific Ocean late on Saturday, dumping heavy rain, ice and snow on the Pacific Northwest, a region still reeling from the last punishing cold front.
"We're going to get pounded," National Weather Service meteorologist Bob Benjamin said.

Flood and storm warnings have been issued from northern California, where more than 10 inches (25 cm) of rain could fall, to Washington state, where 10 inches (25 cm) or more of new snow was in the forecast.
The National Weather Service warned late on Saturday that the Russian and Napa rivers in northern California were likely to rise above flood stage within 24 hours.

Hundreds of utility repair crews raced to restore power to tens of thousands of customers before the full weight of the storm was felt. More than 110,000 homes and businesses remain without electricity due to the Pacific storm that pounded the region on Thursday and Friday.
Puget Sound Power and Light Co., which services nine counties in western Washington state, said about 85,000 of its customers were still without power, down from a peak of nearly 250,000 on Friday.
Puget Power said 185 of its repair crews were working around the clock to restore electricity. Fresh crews were being brought in from as far south as Los Angeles.
"They will work as hard and as fast as they can," said Betty Werblun, a spokeswoman for Puget Power. "But potentially, the incoming storm could undo what we've already done."

A winter storm warning was in effect for much of Washington state. Southwest Washington was expected to see freezing rain mixed with snow. By Sunday night, the Seattle area northward could receive three to 10 inches of new snow, while eight to 12 inches were forecast for the Cascades.

In Oregon, about 25,000 Portland General Electric Co. customers remained without electricity following Thursday's ice storm. Portland General Electric spokesman Kregg Arntson said 200 crews would work through the weekend to restore power to homes and businesses, but he warned changing weather could hamper their efforts. "It (the new storm) has the potential to put us back," Arntson said.

A winter storm warning was issued for the Portland area, which could receive four inches of snow overnight. Snow and freezing rain was reported at Portland International Airport. Snow was even falling along the northwest Oregon coast.
Lowland flooding was reported in northwest Oregon, and all of western Oregon's rivers were under a flood watch. More severe flooding was a possibility on Sunday, forecasters said.
"So far it's a little bit weaker than we thought," said Mark McInerney, a forecaster for the National Weather Service in Portland, of the storm. "But the night is young."

The storm could dump more than 10 inches (25 cm) of rain in the coastal mountains of northern California, forecasters said. Flood watches were issued for most of northern California, where the heaviest rain was expected by early morning.
The National Weather Service issued flood warnings for the Russian and Napa rivers, which were forecast to rise above flood stage Sunday afternoon and night.

Thousands of people living close to the Russian River were preparing for the worst, said Chris Godley, assistant coordinator of the Sonoma County emergency services department. Some residents were stacking sandbags to protect their homes.
Rain from the storm could melt snow in lower mountain areas of California, adding to the potential for dangerous flooding further inland, forecasters said.

In northern California, winds could reach 35 to 45 mph (55 to 70 kph) with gusts to 60 mph (95 kph) in lower elevations, and wind bursts to well over 100 mph (160 kph) over the highest ridges of the Sierra Nevada.
Some wind damage has already been reported in Eureka, California, and strong gusts were recorded in the Sierras.
"It's taking its time getting here," said National Weather Service meteorologist Steve Markkanen from Monterey, California. "But we'll know it when it does."
